blocks.prompt: Why a Basketball Looks the Way It Does
blocks.text: A basketball is not just a plain ball. It is orange so players can see it fast when it flies through the air. It has tiny bumps all over. The bumps are called pebbling. They help your hands hold the ball so it does not slip. Black lines run around the outside. When you shoot, the ball spins, and the lines let you see the spin. Inside, the ball is full of air. That air is the reason it bounces back up every time you push it down.

blocks.prompt: The Cold Day Basketball Was Born
blocks.text: In the winter of 1891, a teacher named James Naismith had a problem. His students in Massachusetts were stuck indoors because it was too cold to play outside. They were bored and restless. Naismith wanted a game they could play in the gym without hurting each other. He thought for a while, then he wrote down thirteen rules. He nailed a peach basket to a railing high on the wall and told the players to toss a ball into it. That was the whole idea, and it worked. There was one funny problem. The bottom of the peach basket was still in place. Every time someone scored, the ball got stuck up there, and a person had to climb up and fetch it. Later they cut the bottom out so the ball could drop straight through. Naismith called his new game basketball. From that one cold day in one small gym, the game spread across the whole world.

blocks.prompt: Nothing About It Is an Accident
blocks.text: A basketball looks simple, but almost everything about it was designed on purpose. Take the color. For the first sixty years, basketballs were brown, and in a dim gym a brown ball blurred into the wooden floor and the crowd behind it. In the late 1950s a coach named Tony Hinkle worked with a sporting goods company to find a color that stood out. They chose orange. The bright ball was easier for players to follow and easier for fans to see, and orange has been the standard ever since. The bounce is not magic either. A basketball is a sealed rubber bladder pumped full of air. When the ball hits the floor, the bottom flattens and squeezes the air inside. Squeezed air pushes back hard, springs the ball back into its round shape, and shoves it upward. If a ball is low on air, it barely bounces, because there is less pressure inside to push back. Players pump each ball to a careful pressure so it bounces the same way every time. Even the bumpy skin has a job. Those tiny raised dots, called pebbling, give sweaty hands something to grip. Without them the ball would slide out of your fingers on a fast shot. The color, the air, the pebbling: every part of the ball was shaped by people solving a real problem on the court.

blocks.prompt: The Game That Kept Fixing Itself
blocks.text: When James Naismith hung a peach basket in a Massachusetts gym in 1891, the game he invented barely resembled the sport played today. His first game had eighteen students, so he split them into two teams of nine. There was no dribbling at all. A player who caught the ball had to stop and throw it to a teammate. The ball itself was a soccer ball, and the basket still had its bottom, so play stopped after every score while someone retrieved the ball. The game changed fast, because players kept finding problems and fixing them. The closed basket was the first thing to go. Cutting out the bottom let the ball drop through and kept the game moving. Teams shrank from nine players to five, which opened up space on the floor. Someone discovered that a player could bounce the ball while moving, and dribbling was born, turning a passing game into a running one. One of the strangest additions had nothing to do with the players. Early hoops were mounted on a balcony railing, and spectators leaning over the edge would reach out and swat away shots aimed at their team's basket. To stop the meddling, officials mounted a solid board behind the hoop. That backboard was meant only as a shield, but players quickly learned to bank shots off it, and it became part of the skill of the game. Basketball spread far beyond that first gym. Teachers carried it around the world, and within a few decades it was played on every continent. In 1936 it became an Olympic sport in Berlin, and Naismith, then in his seventies, was there to watch teams from around the world play the game he had sketched out in an afternoon. What began as a way to keep bored students busy on a cold day had become one of the most popular games on Earth, and it is still changing today.

notes: Naismith wrote thirteen original rules
The ten-foot rim came from a balcony railing
Five-a-side replaced the original nine
The bank shot came from the added backboard

blocks.prompt: The Frame Left Unfinished
blocks.text: Basketball is unusual among major sports because we know exactly who invented it, when, and why. Most games drifted into being over centuries, their true origins lost. Basketball was written down in an afternoon. In December 1891, a physical education instructor named James Naismith was handed a specific assignment: invent an indoor game to keep a class of restless young men active through a New England winter, without the injuries that came with football. He studied the games he already knew, borrowed the best parts, and set down thirteen rules. He nailed a peach basket to a balcony railing ten feet above the floor, and that height, chosen by accident because that is simply where the railing happened to be, remains the official height of the rim today. What makes the story worth telling is not the invention itself but what happened next. Naismith created a skeleton, and everyone who played after him added to it. His first game used a closed basket, so play halted after every score while someone fished the ball out, and that was quickly solved by cutting the bottom away. His first teams had nine players each, because he had eighteen students and simply divided them; five-a-side came later, once players realized that fewer bodies meant more room to move. There was no dribble in the original rules. It appeared when players discovered they could advance the ball by bouncing it, and a passing game became a running one almost overnight. Even the backboard, now central to the sport, began as a fix for a nuisance. Because the early baskets hung from balcony railings, spectators could lean over and knock away shots meant for the other team. Officials mounted a board behind each basket purely to block the interference. Players then discovered they could aim deliberately off that board, and the bank shot entered the game. A defensive shield became an offensive tool, which is a pattern that repeats throughout the sport's history: a rule made for one reason gets used for another. This is the real lesson buried in basketball's origin. A well-designed game is not a finished object but a frame loose enough to keep improving. Naismith seemed to understand this. He never treated his thirteen rules as sacred, and he watched with apparent delight as the game outgrew them. By 1936 basketball was an Olympic sport, and Naismith, in his seventies, traveled to Berlin to see teams from around the world play a game he had scribbled down to fill a cold afternoon. He had built something small and specific, and it became large and universal precisely because he left room for others to change it. The peach basket is long gone. The ten-foot rim, the accident of a railing's height, remains, a small fixed point in a sport that has never stopped rebuilding itself around it.
